items.title: November Update
items.summary: I reckon November is the weirdest month of the year in some respects. You have plenty going on; here, we had Halloween and then Bonfire Night pretty much within the same week.
items.text: Schmookey avatar doing an action pose I reckon November is the weirdest month of the year in some respects. You have plenty going on; here, we had Halloween and then Bonfire Night pretty much within the same week. It's after Bonfire Night that you start to feel that anticipation towards Christmas. In my case, it's a feeling of dread. Meeting the family is fine, and exchanging presents is alright, but it's just the whirlwind of the week and being off schedule. You know the date – just not the day of the week. All your favourite TV shows suddenly air their Christmas specials, and even the random daytime telly gets in on the spirit. On a side note, Christmas TV is filmed long before it's aired. I can't imagine it ever gets easier pretending it's Christmas in April, hoping and praying none of the guests do anything stupid or get caught up in some legal trouble before December. I find myself seeking some sort of solace in my blog again, more as therapy, to just blah blah blah as the words are typed onto the screen (I reckon a new keyboard and mouse could be my Black Friday gift to myself). I am quite happy with some of the aesthetics now. I like that I have been able to sort out music and TV journals. I like giving a snapshot of what I am watching and listening to, albeit it's curated. It's curated so I can force myself to listen to and watch different things. The latest book I'm reading during any spare time is Walking Practice by Dolki Min. It's been wild so far. It's about an alien who landed on Earth and has to find their way to survive. It's a wild ride. I am unashamedly vibes-based. Illustrated book cover for Walking Practice by author Dolki Min I read the blurb, but no more beforehand, as I like to be surprised by the story. The book felt so female-coded initially; I heard the voice of the narrator in my head as a woman. When reading more about the author, I realised they were male, and I was genuinely surprised by my assumption. However, it's also a brilliant sleight of hand by the author. They use this alongside transgender coding to really push the fact that the alien has no gender in the human sense; they can be either male or female depending on the situation. The main character is almost childlike in how self-centred they are and how they can swing from love one minute to "I will murder you" the next. The quote below was my first proper belly laugh in the book, and it set the tone. For context, they are tired, have travelled to get there, and the lift to the other person's apartment is broken. BOOK QUOTATION “He definitely won't come down to the first floor, but do you think, if asked he'd meet me on the eighth and give me a piggyback ride? It would even suffice if he'd get behind me and push” — Walking Practice by Dolki Min 2023 Translated by Victoria Caudle I also added the music function to my vibe-coded multimedia Linux app. It works really well. I was able to get it working with Linux's MPRIS. Basically, it will show the image of my music or audiobook and provide media functions like play, pause and volume controls when the screen is locked. Adding the files feels a bit clunky. I think when I return to it, I'll look into being able to drag and drop the files and whether there is an offline way to create playlists and/or save them. I think once the music component is working in a way I like, I might look at either a PDF function or video function. I am happy with just the EPUB, audiobook and music functions as it is, to be honest, so it might also be the right thing to leave it at that and refine it more. I have also carried out various tweaks to the website and some background SEO/webmaster shenanigans. I also added a trading-card-style profile to the About page. The trading card has clickable links to my other spaces in the Fediverse. I don't really know if the trading card will stay, but I like its interactivity with Fediverse links and microformats, and the ability to make use of so much information in a unique way. I am thinking of more ideas with the website. More of me chatting seems kind of meh, so maybe some short-form reviews of things I've read or watched, and interesting IndieWeb or Fediverse content. I didn't technically go to a fireworks display this year; in a sense, one came to me. I was working late into the night so couldn't attend, but it happened that the big event was happening across from my house. Doggo was not best pleased. That being said, I was able to witness the roaring bonfire and excellent fireworks display. Kai, my doggo, has been unwell recently. I think the fireworks really did a number on his nerves, so I've been keeping an eye on him and giving him extra care and attention. He seems to be coming through the other side now. Promotional image of the full cast from season two of celebrity Traitors UK My TV habits over the past month or so have been Mock the Week, Have You Been Paying Attention? and Celebrity Traitors UK. Wow, Traitors was so much fun to watch. It started off slow, or more accurately, the Richard E. Grant situation felt like its own mini drama, like when a film does a prequel. I loved the Traitor picks this season, though: Maya Jama, proving she will be a television mainstay for years to come; James Acaster – the reluctant Traitor making old Frank Sinatra proud by doing it his way – and King Kenny. He's from the YouTube/TikTok generation of "celebs". I certainly didn't know who he was when he was announced as a contestant. He's knocked it out of the park. I can see him fronting a TV show for young adults on Channel 4 or maybe a slot on BBC Radio 1 or 1Xtra. The drama was there until the end, though. In the final, Kenny got caught out by wanting to stop the voting with four contestants left – it guaranteed he would be voted off. James Blunt misread it in the last three, and he wanted to keep voting when Romesh and Bash wanted to end the game. He sealed his fate with that. His face when he worked out what he'd done. Genuine frustration. I love that Romesh and Bash won. It was a victory for the Faithfuls! I also love that both their charities of choice were for refugees. Absolute right-wing bellends have been villainising refugees over the past couple of years in a blatant attempt at "hey, look over there!" trying to get everyone to look away from the train wreck they themselves have caused with their lazy nativism and ill-thought-out politics. Whoops, I'm ranting... Promotional image of Donald Faison, Zach Braff and Sarah Chalke from the Scrubs Reboot I have also been enjoying the second season of the Scrubs reboot. I love that the focus is still on JD, Turk and Elliot, and it's not just the JD show. The writing has brought out the best of each of the characters whilst also showcasing the younger interns. Two words, though: Nurse Dubois. He's been the glue in the series, and it's been an absolute delight to see the character develop. I've been such a nerd, too, watching their 'making of' shows after each episode. My podcasts lately have all been political to some degree or another because of the US midterms. Yes, they affect us too. Blue-nami indeed. That said, in the US, we have seen this kind of decisive victory before, only for the politicians to be voted out soon after. In the UK, we are used to having a political party ruling for 10+ years and winning successive elections. Will the Democrats get three terms and two presidents, or will it just be another flash in the pan? There is one absolute certainty: they need literal root-and-branch structural change if they wish to even try and keep hold of their modern empire. On a lighter note, sometimes you don't know what you have until it's gone. My toaster went on the blink recently; I just ignored it and decided to wait for a reason to get a new one. Well, my hot water dispenser broke this week. This was my sign: I ordered a new toaster and a kettle on Amazon for next-day delivery. As much as I wasn't missing toast, when I had a slice with peanut butter from the new toaster, it was like meeting an old friend again.

items.title: Coding Vibes
items.summary: Hello you! It's been a while, hasn't it? I know, I know, I just haven't had the same zest and zeal to really keep up to date with the website.
items.text: Home screen from my vibe coded application Hello you! It's been a while, hasn't it? I know, I know, I just haven't had the same zest and zeal to really keep up to date with the website. Firstly, I will say I am no AI evangelist. Those people are the same people who told us Bitcoin was the future and NFTs are worth something. People finding new and interesting ways to part you from your money without offering a service. I do like that AI can be a great aid for jobs and people with disabilities – it shouldn't be seen as a replacement for people. I think about Jevons paradox. Higher demand and lower costs encourage wider adoption and greater overall demand. I don't think this is the end of jobs like coding in the workplace or even bedroom coders. I think it will only be the beginning. Someone with an idea for an app or a fix for something can do it in a weekend instead of a week. People will be able to get through more jobs building apps, software and even SaaS products. People really don't need all the latest computers or the best AI plans. Most of these new products can be made with the help of Chinese AI models, which are really not that far behind their American equivalents, and they are far cheaper to run. Plus, don't discount the majority who are bumming it on OpenAI or Anthropic freemium plans. I think we could potentially be entering a mini golden age of open-source programming alongside the supposed push to download Linux. It will be really interesting to see what comes out of it. There is open-source software like the Adobe alternative ArtCraft, which takes all your Adobe and Microsoft subscription products and offers a very close free version that you can download and keep rather than subscribe to. Logo for the OccupySAAS movement There is also OccupySAAS, who seem very motivated by industry job losses and the rise of AI. They clearly state they don't steal any code and won't use any leaked information. They only use publicly available information. They are currently touting alternatives for Auth0 and Salesforce. The idea of open-source alternatives is not new. LibreOffice, for one, that suite of Word, Excel and PowerPoint alternatives, has been around for some time. Audacity is another. It's basically an entry point for anyone learning to edit audio, and it's incredibly versatile. These are examples of good enough software that can do the majority of the work you need to do. Why aren't they widely used? I think it's the same reason you order a takeaway some nights instead of cooking. Individuals and businesses use Microsoft 365 and Salesforce because they are so ubiquitous and they offer 24/7 support and 99% uptime. They just work – they're always there when you need them. You get a freshly cooked lamb shawarma delivered to your door. The food might be overpriced, and it is probably the same thing you always get, but it's convenient and there when you need it. I also think that millions of applications will be built that never see any kind of public release, or if they do, it's just to show they exist rather than market them for other people's use. I've been on a bit of a kick for some time to purchase and own my own content. I've spoken about this previously on my website. While there are plenty of good ebook reader apps out there, I decided to try and build my own for my own bespoke needs. I wanted something with a moveable sidebar to show chapters, an infinite scroll rather than pages, and a bar at the bottom of the app which shows the chapter number, page number and what percentage I have read of the chapter. I like the percentage bar as it acts like an incentive, whereas if I just saw how many pages I had left in the book overall, it would feel like a chore. The background is black and the text is white to reduce eye strain, and the little affectations like the chapter scroll bar and buttons are green. Ebook function from my vibe-coded application Given that it was fairly straightforward to vibe code, I decided to add a separate audiobook function. There was a load of wrangling! I initially wanted to show the audiobook files separately from the audio player, but it wasn't really handling it well, so I chose to add the chapters below the playback bar, and it worked far better. I set it to save the reading and audiobook positions offline so you can continue where you left off. It was important that I added that function, or the app would be pointless. Audiobook function from my vibe-coded application My philosophy is DRM-free and offline only. I want to promote offline use and using content you've actually bought, rather than licensed content or breaking any Digital Rights Management agreements. I am toying with the idea of adding a music function, but I'm not sure I want it to become an everything app like ArtCraft have created with their versions of the Adobe and Microsoft Office suites. I don't have a problem with what ArtCraft are doing. At least from a technical standpoint, it's a great achievement. I just wonder if my app would be best as a multimedia player or if separate applications are the way forward. You can view it on my Github. I am building it for myself, and it's set to run on Linux through Debian or Flatpak. AI in the right hands, with the right motivation, can be used to genuinely change lives for the better. Data centres can be a good thing if they are used for things like data sovereignty. I can see a future where the internet splinters and becomes more regional or national. With the public pushing for more data sovereignty, and regardless of the US midterm elections, there will be a concerted move in Europe away from the United States towards building more Eurocentric applications, hardware and operating systems. In the UK, we have Ofcom, who regulate our television, radio, broadband and phone services. They started regulating the online space a few years ago. I think this should have been the case from the beginning. While you could argue the "British Internet" would have grown far slower, I would say that it would at least be on more legally sound ground, and initiatives would be in place to help push British services like UK social media platforms, video platforms or search engines, and maybe even a British operating system for your computer. I still think this can happen and honestly hope that it does. We are going through an unprecedented age where we are being manipulated by what we read and see online, and our habits on social media, gaming and pornography are affecting how we live our daily lives. We already have instances on the Fediverse through websites such as Mastodon. You can use the social media platform to create an invite-only and well-moderated space for your school, workplace or lamb shawarma fan club using the ActivityPub protocol in the Fediverse.

items.title: August Updates
items.summary: Hello! I fear it's been a little while, I have updated my NOW page but aside from that I haven't really been online. I tried to write something for the World Cup but it was…
items.text: Illustrated book cover for Automatic Noodle by author Annalee Newitz Hello! I fear it's been a little while, I have updated my NOW page but aside from that I haven't really been online. I tried to write something for the World Cup but it was more waffle than I could handle to post lol. I have been keeping myself under wraps lately. I had a bit of a clarity moment which has sent me on a path to losing some weight, which is no bad thing. 2 and a half stone so far. I have however been finding it difficult to really start things, I am slowly reading Automatic Noodle by Annalee Newitz, It's a fun novelette about robots picking up the pieces following a war. It's a good read but I'm just being slow lately. I've been building up my music collection adding Aaron-Lee Tasjan's latest album Get Over It, Underdog a notable highlight along with Friends in Dark Places by The Black Drumset. I'm currently writing this vibing to an eclectic playlist of Coba-U, Kino and the aforementioned Aaron-Lee Tasjan. My gaming collection has grown significantly, There was a deal to get the Yakuza games 0 through 6 on GOG with a steep discount, as much as I own them already I now have DRM free versions for my computer, I also got Disco Elysium and Turok 1 - 3 I also bought some more DVD's The Wayne's World Collection, Band of Brothers, Teachers boxset, Yes Minister (Prime Minister) oh and Highlander 5 : The Soure. Yes I know but I am totally pilled on the franchise because of the series and what can I say? I do like a bad movie from time to time. I watched the BBC series Ann Droid, great cast including a cameo by Danny John-Jules....Made me smile so hard when I saw him on the show. In terms of movies, I recently watched Lars and the Real Girl. It wasn't what I expected but it was nice to see a movie about a community coming together to help someone. I also watched a German movie called BLOODSUCKERS, Set in the 1920's what if Marx' work was to be taken literally and aristocrats were actual vampires? My local football team made it to the Fifth tier this season, I've been saying I'll go see them but who knows. I have been slowly writing a novel(ette!?), I don't know if it will be any good honestly but I have an idea I need to get out of my head so I'm doing that at a snails pace.

items.title: Physical media
items.summary: For a while I’ve just been coasting along with movies and TV. I used to purchase plenty of DVDs – mainly Asian cinema like Oldboy, Battle Royale, I’m a Cyborg, But That’s OK.…
items.text: An image of a Selection of my film and TV Boxsets" For a while I’ve just been coasting along with movies and TV. I used to purchase plenty of DVDs – mainly Asian cinema like Oldboy, Battle Royale, I’m a Cyborg, But That’s OK. This was before streaming really took off. I would buy them specifically because I wanted to own a copy. Much like the only Blu-ray I’ve ever bought, Ashens and the Polybius Heist, I wanted to contribute to their Indiegogo. Good films I knew wouldn’t be so easy to just watch, and that was a way of doing so while getting something back. It is still wild to me that I’ve had a PS3 since it was released and yet only ever bought one Blu-ray. I guess the extra picture quality wasn’t really a major factor; the important thing was owning a film I wanted to watch whenever I felt like it. It isn’t even like streaming is easier because, honestly, I’ve watched a handful of films on streaming lately. If I’m watching anything via streaming, it’s series or podcasts/vodcasts. I’ve tried too! I’ve taken Mubi, Klassiki and BFI up on streaming deals for annual subscriptions, but I haven’t kept up with them. In terms of other media, I will happily purchase and download digital files for music; there is no DRM, and if I really want to own it, I can buy the CD too. With books, I’m comfortable with eBooks, more than I ever expected. I feel that’s partly to do with being able to customise the look of the page to be more incentivising. I never show the overall number of pages, just pages in each chapter, and I use a bar graphic to show the percentage of the book I’ve read. It breaks down the process for me really well. With video games, I’m happy to play them on Steam, granted after a deep discount most of the time, and I love having GOG. Good Old Games is great because their games are DRM-free. On a few occasions, I have bought a game on Steam and, however long later, when it’s released on GOG, I’ll purchase it again. Recently I’ve had a bit of a kick in purchasing DVD box sets of TV series, pretty much buying them second-hand. DVDs have been around for 30 years now. While DVD players have improved over the years, the discs still hold the same quality, so buying a box set of a show released in 2004 and one in 2024 isn’t really a big issue, albeit with the inherent risk of purchasing second-hand – maybe the previous owner hasn’t been so careful with the discs. The plan is to build up a core of shows I know I’ll keep coming back to time and again, and maybe rip as many of them as I can to a hard drive and build my own Plex server. When I think why – why now? What has changed? – my mind is drawn back to when PlayStation established dominance and there were chunky grey boxes everywhere. I would go around different car boot sales, second-hand video game shops and the like and pick up Sega Mega Drive games for a couple of pounds; even more so, those six-in-one cartridges were common, so you could purchase Alex Kidd and Flicky alongside Shinobi and Columns. During the lifecycle of the PS2, I would go around similar spaces and find old PS1 games, and eBay could be good for a job lot of about 30 games for £20. With the advent of streaming and this whole “you’ll own nothing and like it” culture, it makes me really want to do the opposite. I do want to own some TV series. I want to build up an inexpensive core of DVDs while they are numerous enough. I want to be in control. So far I’ve been trying to focus on British television. It’s my bread and butter, what I’m most used to. It would be nice to hear any thoughts on this. Do you collect physical media? Do you have a favourite place to shop? Are you streaming all the way?

items.title: Podcast blah blah
items.summary: I have been listening to podcasts now for the past 20 years, give or take. It all started with an iPod Classic and finding my favourite weekend radio show was releasing their…
items.text: Image of a Feed icon wearing headphones I have been listening to podcasts now for the past 20 years, give or take. It all started with an iPod Classic and finding my favourite weekend radio show was releasing their content without the music — weird concept, right? Now, I liked the music on their show — very indie, very rock — a lot of great bands on the cusp who sadly would never actually make it. However, it felt like a novel idea that I didn't need to listen to their 3-hour show; I could listen to an 80–90 minute "podcast" on the bus, train, or walking to and from work. You would try and explain them to people and they would just look confused. For me, BBC Radio and NPR were the first great resources, and it was as true then as now that public broadcasters are the most willing to take risks on new "things" — to be ahead of the curve. I also remember having an "iPlayer" day every Monday where I would watch content on BBC iPlayer through my PlayStation 3. This was a great thing because I found things like BBC Click and Storyville. Podcasts were a way to listen to shows that weren't "cool" shows like 'Just a Minute' and look like a weirdo gut-laughing to Adam and Joe on public transport. The spoken-word medium has a knack for making you feel like one of a select few who get to listen or know about it, where the reality is they were cultivating a massive audience. Love him or hate him, Joe Rogan commands a massive fanbase and arguably had a say in more than one U.S. election — yes, I do think that's the peak. Due to the lockdowns of 2020, many comedians in the UK were told they had two choices: write a book or make a podcast... heck, most of TV was basically a video podcast during this period. Your average U.S. talk show just looked like a mid-level podcast setup. I think most production companies realised they have a good stable of talent — let's have them present shows, and we have a ready-made cast of characters to guest those shows. Put them on YouTube, Spotify, and the like, bypass the broadcaster, and keep the income for yourself. While Joe Rogan is at the peak, I think what comes next is oversaturation. I remember when there were five terrestrial TV channels in the UK; now there are so many choices, and yet it can still feel like there is nothing on. With the advent of streaming services, everyone was happy to pay one company £9.99 a month for access to basically everything, and now there are so many streamers and paywalls that people just can't afford it, so don't watch anything. There are like 1,500 football podcasts, 3,000 comedians and their rotating guests, and all your fan-made content too. I don't fault the content — you can throw so much against a wall and you would be surprised at what sticks. The general public are genuinely fickle — they like what they like for no rhyme or reason. There are genuinely some good podcasts/vodcasts out there. We are in a sweet spot, particularly in the UK, where we can get these podcasts for free through places like YouTube, and they have paid-for extra content like "The Rest Is..." Goalhanger shows do. How long until you have to subscribe to listen to them all, though? If and when someone gets that bright idea — and especially if it works for one — they will all try it. I like the BBC's idea about creating a British streaming service — a one-for-all for the likes of the BBC, ITV, Channel 4, and Channel 5. Indeed, this is what BritBox was ultimately supposed to be — like Hulu in the U.S. I think it would be great for the creative industries in the UK if they had this for television, radio, and podcasts alike. I made a podcast for about five minutes a few years ago, and I have been part of others. I've always said that I feel podcasts are the place we can slow down — this is the place where we do have time. How much time? As much as you want! I've taken the idea that it's a great place for discussion and fleshing out ideas and arguments — not your boomer soundbites on the news. Michelle Obama's famous line is "when they go low, we go high"; mine was "if they are tabloid, we are broadsheet". Audio is a great medium because anything can happen — there is nothing stopping the imagination from putting pictures to those words. Right now, my podcast app of choice is AntennaPod. I found it at the right time. A lot of the good podcast players were now charging for quite basic things or including features that felt irrelevant, like file storage, etc. I was becoming more disillusioned with tech in general, so I decided to see if there was any free open-source software I could find and maybe switch fully over to. The AntennaPod app was initially a bit buggy to begin with, but it has really been doing great with each passing update — people who clearly love podcasts looking to make a great app and not make money from it. My current top picks. List by me, image not. Lots of my viewing seems to be done on YouTube these days. I like that some weekend mornings I can wake up and watch J-League football from Japan. I also like that television shows such as the Mock the Week reboot are released online and on their new TV channel — I am more likely to watch it on YouTube because of fewer clicks, I think. I went from watching British basketball all the time when they broadcast exclusively on YouTube to hardly ever since they started primarily broadcasting on DAZN. Some of the bigger basketball matches do get broadcast on YouTube; however, Caledonia Gladiators barely get a look in. I am happy to watch a podcast these days like Rest Is Entertainment or Pablo Torre Finds Out — there is no real difference between watching or listening other than one has visuals. It's not like Torre is juggling fruit. I think it's just a weird preference thing that I will watch some but only listen to others when their content is just sitting and talking. Podcasts are a great example of how nowadays you just need to make content. I remember my lecturer telling us this at college all those years ago when he was showing us a Zoom recorder — one that could also film people. He was talking about how tech was getting better and cheaper all the time. I still have my own audio-only Zoom recorder — expensive, yes, but it paid for itself very quickly. The barrier to entry in the "mediasphere" was already much less expensive, and yet we didn't see TikTok, Twitch, or even what YouTube was to become. Genuinely funny people can now just be funny and end up on shows like SNL UK. I think now that your average celebrity has a podcast of their own and there are big stables even here in the UK, we are at oversaturation. I feel podcasting has already reached its heights; if there are any real paywalls for the content alone, then people will just stop listening. Having them on easy-to-access spaces like YouTube will keep them around for some time, and as long as there are smart people willing to take the time to talk about smart things, people being funny, or there are interesting stories to be told, podcasts will still be here.

items.title: My week 23-29 March
items.summary: This has been a productive week for me online, whislt I have been particularly fiddly with the website, I am in a somewhat happy place with it. I really now just need to get…
items.text: Illustrated book cover for Tower by author Bae Myung-Hoon My Week 23 - 29 March This has been a productive week for me online, whislt I have been particularly fiddly with the website, I am in a somewhat happy place with it. I really now just need to get down to writing more - recording my thoughts. WEBSITE I ended last week well by wrangling with webmentions, a headache until it works. I have subsequently added more of a comment box at the bottom of each blog-type post where people can reply with webmentions form their website, mastodon or wherever they can send a webmention from really. It was a technical thing I was interested in doing because it felt messy and I could get down and dirty with it. There are three buttons above the comments box, back home and archive. self explanitory and felt it right to get that all sorted. I adopted an idea from from sircmpwn and added their Openring 'articles from blogs I follow' to my home page, their hard work on the code and my design over it. It's a great way to show your appreciation for others and hopefully give them new views. I added a more posts elements to my blog posts too; feels like a good way to tie them up together. When I get more posts and tags it can maybe then change to a related posts box. I tweaked my about page to include my Fedivrse socials on it and I added a last played function on the right sidebar, the information is currently inside what looks like an iPod classic, it feels kitsch. It is linked up to my Listenbrainz account. I have removed the guestbook and replaced it with a Now Listening page, It's a way for me to log my listens intentionally. Especially the Listenbrainz weekly exploration playlists. I half expected it to load maybe one or two or to have to play a few songs and see if it worked but it added 90+ songs, I have set it to remove duplicates from being counted. I'm not sure if it will stay, it's likely but maybe in a different form - the important thing is that it works. I had a fairly productive week writing....well this is now my third blog post this week, I have added a changelog and updated my now page. Elsewhere on the web, I've wrangled Brid.gy to some degree, I also signed up for bookwyrm. Reading doesn't come naturally but I have notions here and there, I also have an evergrowning list of titles to read. OTHER MEDIA Not watched major amounts of TV this week, I caught the Wales World Cup qualifer against Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was a tough loss for the Welsh - they had the match in the bag for so long but the Bosnians found a way to take it to penalties and get the win. It's weird being Scottish, I've been used to us for majority of my life either losing in the playoffs or being hopeless in our group. It felt weird to finish top of our group and only need six matches to qualify. If Iraq manage it (for football's sake it would be a wonderful story). They would have had played something like 21 matches to make the 2026 World Cup. Been keeping up with the reboot of Scrubs - can't wait for the next series of Will Trent to air here. I have started watching Sopranos again. Fell asleep watching the Park Chan-Wook directed movie 'No Other Choice' this was my fault and not the film, I started watching it later than I should have. Parts of it feel overly long at the beginning but I love Park Chan-Wook's work so I will definitely need to reschedule and try again. I haven't had much chance to game this week. I started reading tower by Bae Myung-Hoon. A science fiction novel about a nation state of 500,000 people living inside an Empire State type tower block. short interconnected stories inside one larger narrative.

items.title: ListenBrainz
items.text: ListenBrainz, part of the MetaBrainz Foundation Ever since I can remember, I've always had a strong connection with music; I feel emotionally invested. I find it difficult just to have it on passively. I am that person who is constantly fiddling with their device to select songs: "Oh, this song reminds me of that song", "Oh, that band have popped back into my mind, I need to listen." I feel blessed to live in this era where we can carry around gigabytes of music with us in a small box, rather than having to designate time to listen at home or lumber around a massive boombox. Yes, I know Walkmans existed—I had those. However, you were having to carry around the devices, headphones, and your precious CDs or tapes. Just before I was really coming of age with music, we had the whole Limewire, Napster, and the torrenting of music illegally. Now, I don't have an issue with torrenting; I happen to think it is a great way to be able to download content. Ultimately, the more people that like the program, song, or game, the more likely they are to seed. Seeding essentially means everyone has a small piece of the file; 20 seeders all having a small piece each makes it faster and easier for everyone to be able to download it, and no one centralised server is subsequently in control of all of the file. Pirating gave torrenting a bad name in the same way cryptocurrency gives blockchain technology a bad name today—guilt by association. I tend to use places like FOSS Torrents today as a great place to find and download free and open-source software; it's kept up to date and they rely purely on donations and Patreon—they seem to be the textbook definition of doing it for the love of the game. FOSS Torrents I've tried different music services. I subscribed to Spotify back in the day when it was invite-only. Heck, they even followed me on "Elon's Mouthpiece". I was particular about my Last.fm scrobbling. I even had the offline version of the app on my iPod Classic. Oh, how I miss my iPod Classic! I still have it, but the battery died and I've not got round to getting it replaced. For a time, music was throwaway for me. I would find lots of good music, but it just wasn't the same, and honestly I think it's to do with the ease with which we can stream it. It certainly wasn't choice paralysis. I also started using MusicBrainz Picard to help me tag my music better—I'm such a metadata nerd. Nowadays, I primarily use YouTube Music. I already subscribe to their premium service because... screw ads, am I right!? Well, except the ones the creators also put in their videos as part of their content. They were doing the whole "subscribe and get ads anyway" thing before it was "cool". Either way, it doesn't make sense for me to have YouTube and Spotify. I tend to make good use of Bandcamp, though. I've really got back into the idea of ownership—or at least my idea of ownership of digital goods—and not just buying a licence to listen or watch. I will happily buy a physical album too. I've been buying up second-hand DVDs like Blackadder, Monty Python, and Being Human—shows I know I like and want to own physically. I have grand plans of finally setting up a server and making digital copies of all my DVDs, PS1, and PS2 games. Weekly playlist on ListenBrainz Going back to my point on being uptight about getting all my Last.fm listens, recently I decided to try and get back to logging my music again. I settled on using ListenBrainz; it's part of the MetaBrainz group I discussed earlier when I mentioned MusicBrainz Picard. I like the MusicBrainz project because it's open source—it relies on everybody pitching in. Their ListenBrainz team are open about their mission, and they work under the CC0 Creative Commons licence, which essentially puts as much of their work in the public domain as possible. If you scrobble your music with them, they can also give you a weekly playlist of 50 songs—not groundbreaking, I know. However, I have been genuinely impressed with the mix of music it provides: a great mix of classics and modern greats, plus it's been good at throwing in some tracks from left field. One minute you are enjoying Supertramp, and the next, you are bopping your head to Dernière Danse by Indila. As I use YouTube, it means playlists won't just move on to the next song—you need to manually play each song and actively listen. This suits me and my relationship with music. I've really been enjoying listening to music with more intention. A lot of services are opening up to AI music. I am all for AI helping you—at college we were taught Wikipedia can be a good tool as a starting point, but it's not the place to base your research on, simply because it's publicly generated and effectively anyone can edit an article. We were told of a student who did an assignment on libel law; however, it was all about one specific state in the USA and didn't refer at all to our country. WHOOPSIE!!!! AI can give you ideas or some technical help, but using it to effectively write your college paper, news article, or to block government grants for being too "DEI"—whatever that means—is just wild! Much like when a non-techie person buys the latest iPhone but only uses it to text people. They have all the gear but no idea. By all means use it, but it's on you to learn how to use it properly. I saw that OpenAI are closing down Sora—and not a moment too soon, honestly. It's one thing making a funny video of Sam Altman falling down some steps; it's another when it's used by bad actors for propaganda to further their political agenda. "AI" will be a game-changer in Hollywood alongside actors, writers, and directors, but it won't take over from them. I'm really keen to keep on my journey and listen more actively to music. I'd also be keen to know of any streaming suggestions or to chat about music in general.

items.title: My thoughts on SNL UK
items.summary: This weekend, the first episode of the British Saturday Night Live aired. There was an SNL-like show in the 80s called Friday Night Live, before being retitled Saturday Live.…
items.text: Cast of SNL UK This weekend, the first episode of the British Saturday Night Live aired. There was an SNL-like show in the 80s called Friday Night Live, before being retitled Saturday Live. There were some elements of SNL in the show, but there were also significant differences. The show was a launchpad for the likes of TV’s Craig Ferguson, Craig Charles, who later went on to Red Dwarf, and Tracey Ullman, who would ultimately introduce us to The Simpsons. The show helped boost the careers of many of this country’s comedy heavyweights. They have tried to air the US SNL in the UK before on ITV2, but it didn’t gain traction. Most people know of SNL not for the full shows, but because of their ‘Digital Shorts’ and when the production would clip the show’s sketches for YouTube. My first proper experience was Andy Samberg’s Digital Short ‘People Getting Punched Right Before Eating’. It’s dumb internet humour, but also an example of humour telling a great story in three minutes. In the run-up to the show, it felt like they were getting more airtime and interest in the USA than here. While I understand that, it felt like it could be a bad omen. Their UK broadcaster, BSkyB, doesn’t really get the same kind of viewership as the BBC or ITV, but in this day and age it’s all about the clicks. They will make money through social media and gain bigger notoriety. I do like that they’ve skipped a generation and gone with younger talent more suited to TikTok and online virality. It means they will have a better understanding of their potential audience. Also, if this thing pays off, Sky could be raking it in for years—if Larry Dean turns out to be the next Eddie Murphy or Ayoade Bamgboye the next Tina Fey. There are just a few names at the top of this post regarding the cast of the Saturday Live format, and they would be classed as “lesser known” when you look at their full cast list on Wikipedia. This cast could be front and centre for the Comcast-owned Sky schedules for years to come. When you look at that, you’d take those odds: fail and, meh, well, we tried—or succeed, and succeed massively. I watched the first episode on Sunday (yes, I know, I know...). The cold open was very strong and timely—very well written—and honestly captured Keir Starmer perfectly. I would call the Prime Minister beige, but that would be an insult to the colour, honestly. The only thing that kind of irked me was George Fouracres constantly referring to Hammed Animashaun, who was playing our Deputy Prime Minister, as Lammy. I totally get it, though, because despite David Lammy being in Parliament since Tony Blair was in power, he is far less known and has the charisma of a cabbage. The show was, on the whole, very funny. It was biting when it needed to be, particularly during Weekend Update. Jack Shep as Diana, though—what a meme! Absolutely scene-stealing, and he barely had to do anything. Another show that’s crossed the pond—but from Britain this time—is Have I Got News For You, a show that is firmly part of the British comedy furniture. In a lot of respects, the show works in the UK because you have the working-class Paul Merton on one team and the upper-class Ian Hislop on the other. It plays to our class system, but works well when they gang up on that week’s special guest host. They have tried to produce the show in America before, but if you watch clips of it on YouTube, it’s too similar to the UK version—even with the host doing a similar cadence to a lot of the British hosts. This modern version of HIGNFY US has the UK production behind it. They have picked an excellent host in Roy Wood Jr—a host with his own timing and cadence—he’s made it his own. Amber Ruffin on Hislop’s side of the desk—that lady is just funny; she oozes comedy. Michael Ian Black, on Paul’s side, does a great job of keeping the show somewhat grounded while making himself the butt of the jokes. The only bizarre thing about it is that it seems to fit well on CNN, a news network. They satirise the news on a real news network; although, to be fair, is there such a thing as satire these days? From a personal standpoint, I’ve been really happy to see the return of Mock the Week—it’s been really funny. Maybe their four-year hiatus was a good thing, and maybe not having to be as impartial as their time on the BBC has helped. To account for the ad breaks they need now, the show lasts one hour with some extra rounds, and they have worked really well. The panel also seems a bit looser—or maybe that’s just the editing. A sign of the modern times is that I didn’t watch it on their new home, TLC—not once. The channel was smart enough to release the full shows on their YouTube channel. I need to binge the second season of Last One Laughing UK on Amazon. I loved the first one—Bob Mortimer is a legend and deserves to defend his crown. If you get the chance, you should watch the Canadian version; it really is a veritable who’s who of Canadian comedy. You will get to hear about Tom Green’s delicious cheese sandwiches, and, well, Colin Mochrie is in it... need I say more? I hope to see good things from SNL UK for the rest of this series, given the international press it’s had... If they win, British comedy wins.

items.title: Enter The Fediverse
items.summary: I initially set up this website/blog again because I really want to try and fall back in love with the internet—bizarre, I know! The internet has definitely lost something…
items.text: I initially set up this website/blog again because I really want to try and fall back in love with the internet—bizarre, I know! The internet has definitely lost something over the years: its charm. You don’t really see quaint little spaces anymore. It’s all just gambling, adult content, boomers shouting about imaginary crises, and AI slop. The number of worldwide outages that occur because some faceless person in an organisation pressed the wrong button or didn’t debug something correctly—the World Wide Web is far too brittle. This feels similar to our global supply chains: cutting all corners and costs until you’re left with the bare bones, lots of money going to the few but on the back of the content we create. I’ve been on a journey over the past six months or so to consciously decouple myself from as much “big tech” as possible. I started by moving to Linux. I use Linux Mint and honestly, it hasn’t really been all that painful. I can still do 90% of what I did before. The other 10% were only really rare use cases anyway, so it isn’t a loss. I then started looking at open-source or smaller platforms and applications. So, rather than using Google Keyboard, I’m using Futo. Instead of Outlook, I’m using Posteo. I use Listenbrainz and Libre.FM to record most of my music habits. I’ve been using the likes of Libre Office and Audacity for some time. Anyway, I didn’t really intend this to be a listicle. Wow, 10 greatest must-have apps on SlopMOJO!!! I’ve also dipped my toe into the Fediverse. I kind of did so unknowingly before with with Mastodon, when I had that for five minutes after leaving Twitter a few years ago..The Fediverse, is "a decentralised, open-source network of independent social media servers that communicate with each other using shared protocols like ActivityPub," according to Wikipedia. There are decentralised versions of sites like Reddit, Instagram, and Discord—and I mean “like” because it’s the user base that makes the platform, not the technology. You can cross-post between some platforms, so there isn’t the same need to have passwords up to your eyeballs. No single site controls all the information. There are also instances. This is where you create your own version of Piefed or Lemmy and use it for your own ends. So you could have a discussion forum specifically for your school or college, rather than piggybacking off another space and their terms and conditions. This makes you totally liable for the content you post on your instance. While others can’t remove you or your instance, they can remove you from the Federation, but the key is they can’t take your instance away from you. The big takeaway for me is that ActivityPub is an open standard not linked to any one hardware or software platform; services like Mastodon and Lemmy are open-source. They are decentralised and not controlled by an algorithm, and the moderation is dependent on the instance you’re in. Looking at the services, they aren’t filled with conspiracy theorists, etc.; it just seems to be your average person who is done with traditional social media or uses it as part of their social media diet alongside Reddit or X. For my part—when it comes to ownership—I’ve been taking the time to buy old secondhand DVD box sets of TV shows or film franchises. I bought the Godfather trilogy for £4, which is just wild to me! The idea is that I can have more of the shows I watch over and over again close to hand, so I’m not relying on streaming services. I’ve been trying to make a conscious effort to read more. I moved mostly over to Kobo before Amazon locked the ability to download the books you purchased. I prefer reading from an e-reader because it makes me feel less anxious about the whole thing. You can still download your ebooks from Kobo’s desktop site, albeit I’ve definitely become part of the Tsundoku phenomenon—it has actually become a blessing. I prefer ebooks these days. Even audiobooks, I've taken to purchasing them from Libro.fm admittedly usually when a book is on offer—their files are DRM-free. I love music and I’ll do what I can to own the stuff I really enjoy, whether that’s on Bandcamp or other platforms. I’m all in on owning digital copies of albums, but I’ll happily spring for a physical copy too. Like recently, I purchased a physical copy of the FEX album Skyscraper—you don’t get to have the most mysterious song on the internet and get away with it after all!

items.text: Hi! This is my first post… well, here goes! I decided to set up a personal blog again for the first time in years. Lately, I’ve been diving deep into FOSS (Free and Open Source Software) applications ever since I switched to Linux. I finally made the switch, and honestly, it wasn’t as painful as I expected. Even better, I haven’t had to go back to Windows for any apps — which was my biggest worry. I’ve been trying out a bunch of open-source applications and keeping the ones that really work for me. My goal is to free myself from big tech wherever I can and preserve my sanity. Aside from that, I love retro tech, video games, and all things music — so expect some of that here too!. Retro Gamepad
